paras: The attempted lynching of James Redden was a reported effort by residents of the Odessa and Middletown area of New Castle County, Delaware, to lynch Redden, a Black man accused of raping a young girl, on 24–25 February 1882. Wilmington dispatches said officers resisted an organized attempt and took him safely to New Castle jail, but the local Middletown Transcript denied that any attempt was made. Redden was later tried, convicted of rape and hanged at New Castle on 25 August 1882.

Redden, about 25 and known also as 'Loat', was accused of assaulting Sarah (Sallie) Purse, a girl of 13 or 14, at her family's tenement house about a mile and a half from Odessa on Thursday, 23 February, while her parents were away at work. According to the Lancaster Intelligencer's Wilmington dispatch, excitement in the neighborhood was 'intensified by a general belief that justice miscarried' in the recent acquittal of another Black man, William Neal, on a rape charge.

Searchers from Odessa, called a 'vigilance committee' by the Gazette, found Redden on Friday, 24 February; the Transcript named Alexander Moody and Alfred Stevens, acting on a clue from a Black witness, Charles Bristor. The girl identified him, and he was held overnight at Paullin's hotel in Odessa, in the cellar under guard according to the Gazette, before Esquire VanDyke committed him for court.

The Gazette reported that a party formed to lynch him at Odessa but that some members backed out, and that Deputy Sheriff Ash Pennington then took charge of him. While Pennington waited with his prisoner at Middletown for the train, the Gazette said, threats 'were fircely made' and only the train's departure prevented them from being carried out. The Cecil Whig of Elkton, Maryland, told it differently: an 'organized band' searched in vain for the private house where he was hidden, then 'ran madly to the train, too late to secure the prisoner.' Pennington took Redden to New Castle on the late-morning train of Saturday, 25 February, and lodged him in jail.

No arrests of would-be lynchers were reported; Redden claimed an alibi, and the grand jury indicted him for rape in May. At his trial in Wilmington, before a jury of eleven white men and one Black man, he was defended by court-appointed counsel and found guilty after about 19 hours of deliberation. The Chief Justice sentenced him to death, and he was hanged at New Castle jail on 25 August 1882.

Reports of a lynching attempt began in Wilmington and spread by wire: the Lancaster Intelligencer headed the dispatches 'Deserves Death. Dastardly Deed of a Delaware Darkey', and the New-York Tribune 'Attempt to lynch a negro'. The Wilmington Gazette headlined its account 'Another Black Fiend', called the train's departure the thing that 'unfortunately prevented' a lynching, and said 'some of the fiends should be strung up'.

The Middletown Transcript answered that 'There was no movement to lynch him,' charging that Wilmington reporters 'sat in Wilmington' and wrote the story 'hit or miss.' Its editorial page nonetheless said that Redden's not being 'promptly strung up' showed the forbearance of Odessa people, and warned that if he escaped as Neal had, the people would resort to 'the Court of Judge Lynch.' The Smyrna Times took a middle line, reporting 'loud talk of lynching' at Middletown and a constable who used 'great precaution', and a New Castle dispatch printed in the Washington Evening Star on the day of the hanging recalled that threats were made 'but the crowd lacked a leader.'

The case also entered Delaware party politics: the Republican Daily Republican reprinted the Transcript's denial under the heading 'Democratic Hypocrisy', naming the Democratic Every Evening and the Gazette as the papers that 'overdid' the story. A companion editorial mocked the Dover 'Bourbon' paper's 'negrophobia', writing that its custom 'had always been to hang negroes whether guilty or not'. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

Whether any lynching attempt took place is disputed: the Wilmington wire, the Gazette and the Cecil Whig described an attempt or threats, each with different details. The Middletown Transcript, published in the town where the station threats were placed, denied any attempt, saying few people knew of the train and there was 'no unusual crowd at the station'.

accounts.label: Wilmington wire
accounts.gist: An organized attempt to lynch the prisoner was made but was successfully resisted by officers, who took him to New Castle jail.

accounts.label: Wilmington Gazette
accounts.gist: A party formed to lynch him while he was held in the cellar of Paullin's hotel at Odessa but some members backed out; threats were fiercely made at Middletown and only the train's departure prevented them being carried out.

accounts.label: Cecil Whig (Elkton, Md.)
accounts.gist: An organized band sought him overnight at the private house where he was hidden, then ran to the depot too late to take him from the train.

accounts.label: Smyrna Times
accounts.gist: There was loud talk of lynching at Middletown, and the constable used great precaution to keep him from violence.

accounts.label: New Castle execution dispatch (August)
accounts.gist: Redden was arrested in Odessa, 'with some difficulty gotten out of town', and threats of lynching were made, but the crowd lacked a leader.

accounts.label: Middletown Transcript (local)
accounts.gist: There was no movement to lynch him at Odessa or Middletown; the Wilmington reporters wrote 'hit or miss' and few people knew he was taking the train.

framing.detail: The Lancaster Intelligencer ran the Wilmington dispatches under 'Deserves Death. Dastardly Deed of a Delaware Darkey'; the New-York Tribune ran a two-sentence item headed 'Attempt to lynch a negro'.

The Wilmington Gazette headlined 'Another Black Fiend', said only the train's departure 'unfortunately prevented' the threats being carried out, and urged that 'some of the fiends should be strung up'.
The Middletown Transcript denied any lynching attempt and praised Odessa's faith in the courts, while regretting Redden was not 'strung up' and warning of 'Judge Lynch' should he escape.
The Republican Daily Republican reprinted the denial as a rebuke to the Democratic evening papers and mocked the Dover 'Bourbon' paper's 'negrophobia'.
